Breast Volume Guide — How to Estimate and Understand Your Breast Volume

Evidence-based guide to breast volume estimation. Understand cc ranges per cup size, how volume relates to weight, and how to use volume for bra selection.

What Is Breast Volume?

Breast volume is the three-dimensional space occupied by one breast, typically measured in cubic centimeters (cc) or milliliters (mL). One cc equals one mL. Volume is a more precise descriptor of breast size than cup size alone, because two women with the same cup size can have very different volumes depending on band size, projection, and breast shape.

Clinical Measurement Methods

Medical research uses three gold-standard methods to measure breast volume:

1. MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging)

MRI is the most accurate non-invasive method. It captures a full 3D model of the breast and gives volumes accurate to within 3–5% [1] . It is expensive and not used outside research or surgical planning.

2. Water Displacement (Archimedes' Principle)

The breast is submerged in a calibrated water tank; the volume of water displaced equals the breast volume. This is the historical gold standard for surgical research and is accurate to within 5–8%. It is impractical for everyday use.

3. 3D Surface Scanning

Modern 3D scanners create a virtual model of the breast surface, from which volume is computed. This is the method used in current bra-fitting research and is accurate to within 5–10% [3] .

The BREAST-V Formula

For everyday use, the BREAST-V formula provides a reliable estimate without any specialized equipment:

Volume (cc) = 15.6 × Base Width (cm) × Nipple-to-IMF (cm) × Projection (cm) − 142.5

This formula was developed using 3D scanning data from 605 patients and is accurate to within ±10–15% in the precise mode of our Breast Volume Calculator [2] .

Average Volume per Cup Size

The following ranges come from clinical studies of Caucasian and East Asian women. Individual variation is significant.

Cup Size Volume per breast (cc) Notes
AA 80–120 Small, often shallow projection
A 120–200 Narrow root, modest projection
B 200–320 Versatile; many styles fit
C 320–460 Average range; full support needed
D 460–700 Reconstruction / reduction thresholds
DD / E 700–900 Reinforced band essential
DDD / F 900–1200 Specialty construction needed
G+ 1200+ Custom or specialty fitters recommended

East Asian women tend to have slightly smaller average volumes (~340 cc per breast) and a higher proportion of shallow-projection shapes compared to Western populations [2] .

How Volume Helps Bra Selection

Cup size is a proxy for volume, but it is not the whole story. Two women with the same band and cup can have different volumes if their breast shape is different. By knowing your volume in cc, you can:

  • Compare bra styles and brands with different cup conventions (US vs UK vs EU)
  • Calibrate the Breast Volume Calculator against your known bra size
  • Make informed decisions about reduction or augmentation surgery (always consult a surgeon for clinical decisions)

FAQs

Is volume the same as weight?

No. Volume is space (cc); weight is mass (grams). To convert, multiply volume by tissue density (~0.94 g/cc for breast tissue). Use our Breast Weight Calculator for a complete estimate.

Why is my left breast a different size from my right?

Asymmetric breasts are extremely common. Studies show that more than 88% of women have some degree of asymmetry, and the difference averages about 50–100 cc. Use the larger breast as your reference size.

Can I measure volume at home?

Not directly. The BREAST-V formula (using three tape measurements) gives an estimate accurate to ±10–15%, which is good enough for bra fitting but not for surgical planning. For clinical decisions, consult a plastic surgeon who can order an MRI or 3D scan.
